usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger person
banmal, to a close friend or child
examples: A: 시험 100점 받았어요 / B: 와, 잘했어요!
A: I got 100 on the test / B: Wow, well done!
the bare praise as an instant reaction to good news
발표 끝나고 부장님이 "수고했어, 잘했어" 하셨어요.
After the presentation the manager said, 'Good work, well done.'
everyday: a senior praising a junior, so banmal flows downward
애기가 혼자 신발 신었을 때 "우와, 잘했어! 최고야" 하고 칭찬했어요.
When the kid put on shoes alone I praised, 'Wow, good job! You're the best.'
real situation: praising a child, paired with 최고야 for encouragement
nuance: 잘했어요 is the everyday 'well done' you say AFTER someone has finished or achieved something — it judges a completed action, built from 잘 'well' + 했다, the past of 하다 'to do'. Crucially it flows DOWNWARD or sideways: a senior to a junior, a parent to a child, friends to each other. The decisive line is against 잘하시네요, which praises ongoing SKILL ('you're good at this') in the present, while 잘했어요 praises a finished result. The English-speaker pitfall is firing 잘했어요 UP at a boss or teacher: praising a superior's performance sounds presumptuous, like you are grading them. To an elder you respect, fold in 시 as 잘하셨어요, but even then heap-praising a senior's work is best softened into thanks (수고하셨어요) rather than evaluation. Register-shift is simply 잘했어 (banmal) ↔ 잘했어요 (polite) ↔ 잘하셨어요 (honorific).

mistakes: Saying 잘했어요 to your boss about their own work — evaluating a superior sounds condescending; thank them with 수고하셨어요 instead of grading them.
Confusing 잘했어요 (a finished action: 'you did well') with 잘하시네요 (a present skill: 'you're good') — wrong one makes you praise the wrong thing.
Writing 잘 했어요 with a space — as a fixed praise expression it is written together, 잘했어요; the spaced 잘 했어요 reads as the literal 'did it well'.

examples: A: (그림을 보여주며) / B: 와, 잘하시네요!
A: (showing a drawing) / B: Wow, you're really good!
the bare admiring reaction to a skill on display
요리 한 입 먹고 "어머, 요리 잘하시네요" 했어요.
After one bite I said, 'Oh my, you're a great cook.'
everyday: complimenting a host's cooking with the -시- form
한국어로 인사하니까 직원분이 "한국말 진짜 잘하시네요" 하고 놀랐어요.
When I greeted in Korean the staff was surprised: 'Your Korean is really good.'
real situation: the go-to compliment Koreans give learners; respond with 아니에요
nuance: 잘하시네요 is the present-tense 'you're good at this' you say WHILE watching or tasting someone's skill — 잘하다 'to do well' + honorific -시- + the noticing ending -네요 ('oh, I notice'). It praises ABILITY in the moment, not a finished result, which is the dividing line from 잘했어요 ('you did a good job' on something already done). Because -시- and -네요 are baked in, 잘하시네요 politely points UP or sideways, so unlike 잘했어요 it is safe toward someone older or a stranger. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: dropping the -시- and saying 잘하네 to an elder (too casual), and treating the very common 한국말 잘하시네요 as a literal report — it is a warm icebreaker, and the natural Korean reply is the modest 아니에요, 아직 멀었어요, never 네, 잘해요. Register-shift: 잘하네 (banmal) ↔ 잘하네요 (polite) ↔ 잘하시네요 (honorific).

Saying 잘하네 to someone older — the bare -네 is banmal; toward a senior you need the honorific 잘하시네요.

english: That's cool / You look great / How impressive.
usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger
exclamatory -다, said to yourself out loud
examples: A: (새 차를 보여주며) / B: 와, 멋있어요!
A: (showing a new car) / B: Wow, that's awesome!
the bare reaction to something impressive or stylish
무대에서 춤추는 거 보고 "오빠 진짜 멋있어" 했어요.
Watching him dance on stage I said, 'You're so cool.'
everyday: 멋있다 praises style, vibe, or a cool action
선배가 후배 도와주는 거 보고 "선배님, 정말 멋있으세요" 했어요.
Seeing the senior help a junior I said, 'You're truly admirable, sunbae.'
real situation: 멋있다 also praises admirable CHARACTER, not just looks
nuance: 멋있어요 means 'cool / stylish / impressive' and stretches from a sharp outfit and a slick car to an admirable ACTION or character ('that was a cool thing to do'). Note the split learners miss: 멋있다/멋지다 lean toward cool, dashing, impressive (often men, or anyone's cool deed), while 예쁘다 means pretty/cute (people, objects) — they are not interchangeable. The decisive line is 멋있다 (cool, impressive) vs 예쁘다 (pretty, lovely): a tuxedo and a brave act are 멋있다, a flower and a baby are 예뻐요. The English-speaker pitfall is overusing 'cool' as filler — Korean 멋있다 is a real compliment with weight, so dropping it constantly dilutes it; and many forget the honorific 멋있으세요 when admiring an elder's character. 멋있다 and 멋지다 are near-twins; 멋지다 sounds a touch more exclamatory ('how splendid'). Register: 멋있어 (banmal) ↔ 멋있어요 (polite) ↔ 멋있으세요 (honorific).

mistakes: Calling a flower or a baby 멋있어요 — that is 예뻐요; 멋있다 is for cool/impressive things and people, not cute ones.
Saying 멋있어 to an elder you respect — use the honorific 멋있으세요 when praising a senior's looks or character.
Spelling it 맛있어요 (delicious) by mistake — 멋 (style) vs 맛 (taste); one vowel flips 'cool' into 'tasty'.

usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger
examples: A: (새 옷을 입고) / B: 우와, 예뻐요!
A: (in new clothes) / B: Wow, that's pretty!
the bare compliment on appearance or an item
꽃다발 받고 "꽃 너무 예쁘다" 하면서 좋아했어요.
Getting the bouquet I happily said, 'The flowers are so pretty.'
everyday: 예쁘다 covers objects, flowers, and people
아기 사진 보고 "어머, 아기 너무 예뻐요" 했더니 엄마가 좋아했어요.
Seeing the baby photo I said, 'Oh, the baby is so adorable,' and the mom loved it.
real situation: 예쁘다 for cute babies — a warm, safe compliment to a parent
nuance: 예뻐요 means 'pretty / lovely / adorable' and applies to people, clothes, flowers, babies, handwriting — anything visually pleasing or cute. The base 예쁘다 is a 으-irregular: drop 으, add 어요 → 예뻐요 (not 예쁘어요). The dividing line is against 귀엽다 'cute' and 멋있다 'cool': 예쁘다 = pretty/lovely, 귀엽다 = cutely endearing (puppies, a giggling toddler), 멋있다 = cool/impressive — calling a strong handsome man 예뻐요 can sound off, where 멋있어요 fits. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation (saying 예쁘어요) and over-aiming it at strangers: complimenting a stranger's looks can feel forward in Korean, so 예뻐요 is warmest toward friends, items, or kids. To an older woman, soften with the honorific 예쁘세요. Register: 예뻐 (banmal) ↔ 예뻐요 (polite) ↔ 예쁘세요 (honorific).

mistakes: Conjugating it 예쁘어요 — 예쁘다 is a 으-irregular, so 으 drops before 어요: the correct form is 예뻐요.
Calling a cool, manly guy 예뻐요 — it implies pretty/feminine; use 멋있어요 for cool or handsome men.
Complimenting a stranger's face with 예뻐요 out of nowhere — it can feel forward; aim it at friends, kids, or objects, or compliment an outfit instead.

examples: A: 마라톤 완주했어요 / B: 와, 대단하세요!
A: I finished the marathon / B: Wow, that's amazing!
the bare awe-reaction to an impressive feat
혼자 애 셋 키운다는 말에 "진짜 대단하세요" 했어요.
Hearing she raises three kids alone I said, 'You're truly amazing.'
everyday: admiring someone's effort or endurance
사장님이 맨손으로 회사 키운 얘기 듣고 "정말 대단하십니다" 했어요.
Hearing the boss built the company from nothing I said, 'That's truly remarkable, sir.'
real situation: the formal -십니다 to a respected senior
nuance: 대단하세요 expresses genuine AWE at someone's achievement, effort, or ability — 대단하다 'to be remarkable/great' + honorific -세요. It is heartfelt admiration for something hard ('I couldn't do that'), so it naturally points UP at people you respect, which is why the -세요 honorific form is the default. The dividing line is against 잘하시네요: 잘하시네요 praises a SKILL ('you're good at this'), while 대단하세요 expresses being IMPRESSED by the whole accomplishment or person ('that's incredible'). The English-speaker pitfall is the bare 대단해 toward an elder — fine between friends, but to a senior it sounds flippant, so you need 대단하세요 or formal 대단하십니다. A subtler trap: 대단하다 can turn sarcastic with a flat tone ('oh, great...'), so deliver it warmly. Register: 대단해 (banmal) ↔ 대단해요 (polite) ↔ 대단하세요 / 대단하십니다 (honorific/formal).

Using 대단하세요 for a minor everyday compliment — it carries real awe, so reserve it for genuinely impressive feats, not 'nice shoes'.
Delivering it flatly — 대단하다 can read as sarcasm ('oh, wonderful'); say it with clear warmth so it lands as praise.

english: Go for it! / You can do it! / Good luck!
usage: go for it / you got this
the officially correct spelling, same word
examples: A: 나 이제 면접 보러 가 / B: 화이팅!
A: I'm off to my interview / B: Go get 'em!
the bare one-word cheer before a challenge
시험 보는 친구한테 "내일 시험 화이팅!" 하고 메시지 보냈어요.
I texted my friend, 'Good luck on the exam tomorrow!'
everyday: the standard text of encouragement before a test
선배 마라톤 나간다고 해서 "선배님, 화이팅 하세요!" 하고 응원했어요.
Since my senior was running a marathon I cheered, 'Go for it, sunbae!'
real situation: add 하세요 to cheer politely for someone older
nuance: 화이팅 (from English 'fighting') is Korea's all-purpose cheer of encouragement — 'go for it, you've got this, good luck' — fired before exams, interviews, games, or any effort, often with a raised fist. By itself it is casual and friendly; toward someone you respect, attach a verb as 화이팅 하세요 ('please do your best'). The dividing line is against 잘될 거예요: 화이팅 pumps up ENERGY for the effort ahead ('push!'), while 잘될 거예요 reassures about the OUTCOME ('it'll turn out fine'). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: it means encouragement, NOT literal combat, so never read it as 'let's fight'; and the bare 화이팅 to a much older person or in a formal setting feels too light — use 화이팅 하세요 or 잘하시길 바랍니다. Spelling note: 파이팅 is the National-Institute-correct spelling, but 화이팅 is what most people actually write. There is no honorific form of the noun itself — politeness rides on the attached verb.

english: Cheer up / Stay strong / Hang in there.
usage: polite -세요, to a peer or someone you respect
stay strong, it'll all be okay
examples: A: 요즘 너무 힘들어요 / B: 힘내세요.
A: Things are so hard lately / B: Stay strong.
the bare encouragement to someone struggling
시험 떨어진 친구한테 "너무 속상해하지 말고 힘내" 했어요.
I told my friend who failed, 'Don't be too upset, hang in there.'
everyday: comforting a friend after a setback in banmal
상을 당한 동료에게 "많이 힘드시죠. 힘내세요" 하고 위로했어요.
To a grieving colleague I said, 'This must be so hard. Stay strong,' as comfort.
real situation: gentle encouragement in grief, paired with empathy
nuance: 힘내세요 literally 'put out strength' (힘 'strength' + 내다 'to bring out' + -세요) is the warm 'cheer up / hang in there / stay strong' you give someone who is tired, sad, or going through a hard time. It is encouragement during ONGOING hardship, which is the dividing line from 화이팅 (a pre-event pump-up) and 잘될 거예요 (reassurance about the result). The English-speaker pitfall is register and tone: bare 힘내 is banmal for friends, while a struggling senior or colleague needs 힘내세요. A deeper trap is using it in heavy grief — at a funeral, 힘내세요 can feel like pressure to 'snap out of it', so for serious loss Koreans prefer 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 or 얼마나 힘드세요 (acknowledging the pain) before any 힘내세요. Don't pair it with a literal 'fight' image. Register-shift: 힘내 (banmal) ↔ 힘내세요 (polite) ↔ 힘내십시오 (formal).

english: Good work / Thanks for your effort.
usage: polite -요, to a peer or junior
banmal, to a close friend or junior
thank you for your hard work
formal honorific, to a senior or in business
you went through a lot / well done
examples: A: 일 다 끝냈어요 / B: 수고했어요.
A: I finished all the work / B: Good work.
the bare acknowledgement when someone wraps up a task
퇴근하면서 동료에게 "오늘도 수고했어요" 하고 인사했어요.
Leaving work I said to a colleague, 'Good work again today.'
everyday: the standard end-of-day workplace farewell
발표 끝난 후배한테 "준비하느라 고생 많았어, 수고했어" 했어요.
To the junior after the presentation I said, 'You worked hard preparing — good job.'
real situation: acknowledging effort, pairs with 고생 많았어
nuance: 수고했어요 (수고 'effort/trouble' + 했어요) thanks and acknowledges someone for the EFFORT they put in — said after a task, a shift, or a hard day, and as a routine 'good work' when leaving the office. The critical rule is DIRECTION: 수고했어요/수고하셨습니다 normally flows to peers or DOWN to juniors, and saying 수고하셨습니다 to a clear superior is debated — many feel a junior shouldn't 'evaluate' a boss's labor, so to a higher-up 감사합니다 is safer. The dividing line from 고생했어요 is tone: 고생했어요 stresses the toil/suffering ('you went through a lot') and feels warmer, while 수고했어요 is the neutral standard. The English-speaker pitfall is using bare 수고했어 upward (too casual and presumptuous) and overusing it to a boss where thanks fits better. Register: 수고했어 (banmal) ↔ 수고했어요 (polite) ↔ 수고하셨습니다 (formal).

Register: 수고했어 (banmal) to 수고했어요 (polite) to 수고하셨습니다 (formal).

mistakes: Saying 수고했어요 to your boss or a clear senior — it can read as a junior grading their effort; use 감사합니다 or 고생 많으셨습니다 carefully instead.
Using bare 수고했어 with a senior — drop to 수고하셨습니다; the banmal upward is rude.
Treating 수고하세요 (to someone still working / leaving) and 수고했어요 (to someone who finished) as the same — present 하세요 vs past 했어요 changes the meaning.

usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger
examples: A: 저 합격했어요! / B: 와, 축하해요!
A: I passed! / B: Wow, congratulations!
the bare congratulation as an instant reaction
친구 결혼한다고 해서 "결혼 진심으로 축하해" 했어요.
Since my friend is getting married I said, 'Congratulations on your wedding, truly.'
everyday: name the occasion + 축하해, with 진심으로 for sincerity
부장님 승진 소식에 "승진 축하드립니다" 하고 인사했어요.
On the manager's promotion I said, 'Congratulations on your promotion, sir.'
real situation: to a senior, the humble 축하드립니다 is the respectful choice
nuance: 축하해요 (祝賀, 축하 'congratulation' + 해요) is the all-purpose 'congratulations' for any happy milestone — passing, a wedding, a promotion, a birthday. The key politeness move is the humble verb: to an elder, a boss, or in formal settings you swap 하다 for 드리다 → 축하드려요 / 축하드립니다 ('I offer my congratulations'), which is more respectful than plain 축하해요. The dividing line is 축하해요 (neutral polite, peers) vs 축하드립니다 (humble formal, upward). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle and word order: learners say 축하해요 그 일 or attach 을/를, but the natural pattern names the occasion FIRST, e.g. 합격 축하해요, 생일 축하해요 — the thing being celebrated comes before 축하해요, with no object particle needed in speech. Also avoid bare 축하해 to a senior. Register: 축하해 (banmal) ↔ 축하해요 (polite) ↔ 축하드립니다 (humble/formal).

Word order like 축하해요 생일 — the occasion comes first: 생일 축하해요, 합격 축하해요.
Adding an object particle (합격을 축하해요 in casual speech) — in everyday talk it is just 합격 축하해요, no 을/를 needed.

usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger
격식 -합니다, a card or formal setting
examples: (케이크 앞에서) 생일 축하해요!
(in front of the cake) Happy birthday!
the bare birthday greeting as the candles go out
친구한테 "생일 축하해! 선물 준비했어" 하고 건넸어요.
I said to my friend, 'Happy birthday! I got you a present,' and handed it over.
everyday: the casual banmal greeting with friends
할머니께 "할머니, 생신 축하드려요. 건강하세요" 하고 인사드렸어요.
To grandma I said, 'Happy birthday, grandma. Stay healthy.'
real situation: 생신 is the honorific word for an elder's birthday
nuance: 생일 축하해요 is 'happy birthday' (생일 'birthday' + 축하해요 'congratulations'). The single most important upgrade for learners is the honorific noun: an elder's birthday is 생신, not 생일, so to grandparents, parents, or a respected senior you say 생신 축하드려요 / 생신 축하드립니다 — using plain 생일 for a grandparent sounds under-polite. The dividing line is exactly 생일 (neutral/peers/juniors) vs 생신 (honorific, for elders), paired with 해요 vs 드려요. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'happy' literally with 행복한/즐거운 — Korean does NOT say 행복한 생일; it is built on 축하 'congratulate', so it is 생일 축하해요, never a 'happy + birthday' calque. Also don't forget the space: 생일 and 축하해요 are separate words. To make it warmer, friends add 진심으로 or sing 생일 축하합니다. Register: 생일 축하해 (banmal) ↔ 생일 축하해요 (polite) ↔ 생신 축하드립니다 (honorific/formal).

english: It'll work out / Things will be fine.
usage: polite -요, reassuring a peer or younger
examples: A: 합격할 수 있을까요? / B: 잘될 거예요.
A: Do you think I'll pass? / B: It'll work out.
the bare reassurance about an uncertain outcome
걱정하는 친구한테 "너무 걱정 마, 다 잘될 거야" 했어요.
To my worried friend I said, 'Don't worry too much, it'll all work out.'
everyday: pairs naturally with 너무 걱정 마
수술 앞둔 분께 "분명히 잘되실 거예요. 응원할게요" 하고 위로했어요.
To someone facing surgery I said, 'It'll surely go well. I'm rooting for you.'
real situation: honorific 잘되실 거예요 + 응원할게요 for serious comfort
nuance: 잘될 거예요 ('it will go well', 잘되다 'to turn out well' + future -ㄹ 거예요) reassures someone about a FUTURE OUTCOME they are anxious about — a test result, a job, a recovery. The dividing line is clear: 잘될 거예요 calms worry about how things will TURN OUT, while 힘내세요 gives strength for the present struggle and 화이팅 pumps energy for the effort itself; the smoothest comfort stacks them ('너무 걱정 마세요, 잘될 거예요'). The English-speaker pitfall is the verb and spelling: it is 잘되다 (one word, intransitive 'turn out well'), so 잘될 거예요 — not 잘할 거예요, which means 'I/you WILL do well' (an action by a doer), a different meaning. Also the future ending is 거예요 (not 꺼에요/거에요). To an elder, raise it with -시- as 잘되실 거예요. Register: 잘될 거야 (banmal) ↔ 잘될 거예요 (polite) ↔ 잘되실 거예요 (honorific).

usage: polite -세요, to a peer or someone you respect
reassurance plus an offer of help
examples: A: 일이 잘못될까 봐 불안해요 / B: 너무 걱정 마세요.
A: I'm anxious it'll go wrong / B: Don't worry too much.
the bare reassurance to calm someone's anxiety
시험 걱정하는 동생에게 "너무 걱정 마, 넌 충분히 잘했어" 했어요.
To my anxious younger sibling I said, 'Don't worry, you did plenty well.'
everyday: comfort in banmal, paired with praise
환자 보호자분께 "너무 걱정 마세요. 최선을 다하겠습니다" 하고 안심시켰어요.
To the patient's guardian I said, 'Please don't worry. We'll do our best,' to reassure them.
real situation: professional reassurance with a commitment
nuance: 너무 걱정 마세요 ('don't worry too much', 너무 'too' + 걱정 'worry' + 마세요 'please don't') tells an anxious person to ease off their worry, usually paired with a reason or 잘될 거예요. 마세요 is the contracted polite prohibitive of 말다; the full form 걱정하지 마세요 is identical in meaning and a touch softer/more careful. The dividing line is against 잘될 거예요: 걱정 마세요 addresses the WORRY directly ('stop fretting'), while 잘될 거예요 addresses the OUTCOME ('it'll be fine') — they pair beautifully. The English-speaker pitfall is the negative command itself: learners build it from 안 ('안 걱정하세요' is wrong) instead of the prohibitive 말다; and they say bare 걱정 마 to an elder. Keep 너무 — without it, 걱정 마세요 alone is fine but a bit blunt; 너무 softens it to 'don't worry SO much'. Register: 걱정 마 (banmal) ↔ 걱정 마세요 (polite) ↔ 걱정 마십시오 (formal).

usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger
banmal, to a close friend or child
격식 -습니다, a speech or formal note
네가 names who you're proud of
examples: A: 저 1등 했어요 / B: 우와, 자랑스러워요!
A: I came in first / B: Wow, I'm so proud!
the bare expression of pride at someone's success
졸업한 딸에게 "우리 딸, 정말 자랑스러워" 했어요.
To my graduating daughter I said, 'I'm so proud of you, my girl.'
everyday: a parent's pride in banmal toward a child
후배가 큰 상 받았을 때 "네가 우리 팀의 자랑이야. 정말 자랑스러워" 했어요.
When the junior won a big award I said, 'You're our team's pride. I'm truly proud.'
real situation: pairs with 자랑이야 'you're our pride'
nuance: 자랑스러워요 ('to be proud', from 자랑 'pride/boast' + -스럽다 'to feel like') expresses pride in someone's achievement or in someone you care about. The crucial cultural rule is DIRECTION: you express pride DOWNWARD or sideways — a parent to a child, a senior to a junior, friends to each other. Telling a teacher, boss, or elder 자랑스러워요 sounds odd, even presumptuous, as if you were positioned above them; toward a respected senior, Koreans instead say 존경스러워요 ('I admire/respect you') or 대단하세요. That is the dividing line: 자랑스럽다 (pride, looking down/across) vs 존경스럽다 (respect, looking up). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this — English 'I'm proud of you' is said freely to anyone, so learners aim 자랑스러워요 at their Korean teacher and it lands wrong. Note the -ㅂ irregular: 자랑스럽다 → 자랑스러워요. Register: 자랑스러워 (banmal) ↔ 자랑스러워요 (polite) ↔ 자랑스럽습니다 (formal).

english: That looks nice / It's good to see.
usage: it looks nice / good to see
polite -요, to a peer or younger
examples: A: (커플 사진을 보여주며) / B: 와, 보기 좋아요.
A: (showing a couple photo) / B: Aw, you look great together.
the bare warm comment on a pleasant sight
살 빠진 친구한테 "얼굴 좋아 보인다, 보기 좋아" 했어요.
To my friend who lost weight I said, 'You look well — looks good.'
everyday: complimenting someone's healthier look
오랜만에 만난 두 분이 사이좋게 지내셔서 "두 분 보기 좋으세요" 했어요.
Seeing the two get along well I said, 'It's lovely to see you two together.'
real situation: honorific 보기 좋으세요 toward elders, approving warmly
nuance: 보기 좋아요 (보다 'to see' + -기 nominalizer + 좋다 'good' = 'good to look at') is the warm 'that looks nice / it's nice to see' you say about a pleasing sight — a happy couple, someone looking healthy, a tidy room, people getting along. It often carries APPROVAL of a wholesome scene, not just visual prettiness, which is the dividing line from 예뻐요 (pretty appearance) and 멋있어요 (cool/impressive): 보기 좋다 = 'this is a good thing to see / heartwarming'. The English-speaker pitfall is the structure — learners try 좋게 보여요 or 좋아 보기, but the fixed form is 보기 좋다 (nominalized 보기 + 좋다). Also it sits next to the look-like form 좋아 보여요 ('looks good/well'), which describes condition; don't confuse 보기 좋다 ('nice to see') with 좋아 보이다 ('appears good'). To an elder, use the honorific 보기 좋으세요/좋으시네요. Register: 보기 좋아 (banmal) ↔ 보기 좋아요 (polite) ↔ 보기 좋으세요 (honorific).

english: I'm jealous / I envy you (in a good way).
usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger
examples: A: 저 다음 주에 하와이 가요 / B: 와, 부러워요!
A: I'm going to Hawaii next week / B: Wow, I'm so jealous!
the bare good-natured envy as a reaction to good news
친구가 새 집 샀다고 해서 "우와, 진짜 부럽다" 했어요.
Since my friend bought a new house I said, 'Wow, I'm so jealous.'
everyday: a warm compliment dressed as envy, in banmal
동안인 선배한테 "피부가 너무 좋으세요. 부러워요" 했어요.
To my youthful-looking senior I said, 'Your skin is so good. I'm jealous.'
real situation: envy used as a friendly compliment about looks
nuance: 부러워요 ('I'm envious', from 부럽다 'to be enviable') is, in Korean, a FRIENDLY compliment far more often than a complaint — said brightly, it means 'lucky you, I wish that were me' and warmly congratulates someone's good fortune (a trip, a new house, nice skin). The dividing line is against 질투하다 (jealousy that resents) and 샘나다 (petty envy): 부럽다 is the harmless, admiring kind, so it functions as praise, while 질투 implies real ill feeling. The English-speaker pitfall is conjugation and tone: 부럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular → 부러워요 (not 부럽어요); and learners worry it sounds negative like English 'jealous', but with a smile it is a beloved compliment, so don't avoid it. Saying it flatly, though, can tip into sounding genuinely resentful, so deliver it lightly. Register: 부러워 (banmal) ↔ 부러워요 (polite) ↔ 부럽습니다 (formal).

From 부럽다 'to be enviable'.
부럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular, giving 부러워요 (not 부럽어요). Register: 부러워 (banmal) to 부러워요 (polite) to 부럽습니다 (formal).

The English-speaker pitfall is conjugation and tone: learners worry it sounds negative like English 'jealous', but with a smile it is a beloved compliment, so don't avoid it. Saying it flatly, though, can tip into sounding genuinely resentful, so deliver it lightly.

mistakes: Conjugating it 부럽어요 — 부럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular: the correct form is 부러워요.
Avoiding it because 'jealous' sounds negative — said with a smile, 부러워요 is a warm compliment ('lucky you'), not a complaint.
Using 질투해요 to mean friendly envy — 질투 is resentful jealousy; the admiring kind is 부러워요.

english: I'll be rooting for you / I've got your back.
usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger
I'll always be rooting for you
항상 makes it a lasting promise
examples: A: 저 도전해 보려고요 / B: 응원할게요!
A: I'm going to give it a try / B: I'm rooting for you!
the bare pledge of support for someone's effort
시험 보는 친구한테 "내가 응원할게, 잘할 수 있어" 했어요.
To my friend taking the exam I said, 'I'm rooting for you, you can do it.'
everyday: support in banmal, paired with belief in them
퇴사하고 창업한다는 선배께 "새로운 시작 진심으로 응원하겠습니다" 했어요.
To the senior starting a business I said, 'I sincerely support your new beginning.'
real situation: formal 응원하겠습니다 for a serious life step
nuance: 응원할게요 (應援, 응원 'support/cheering' + -ㄹ게요 'I will (for you)') is a personal pledge — 'I'll cheer you on, I'm in your corner' — promising ongoing support for someone's effort or challenge. It is warmer and more committed than 화이팅: 화이팅 is a quick shout in the moment, while 응원할게요 promises that YOU will keep backing them. The -ㄹ게요 ending is itself a speaker's promise, so it always implies 'I, for your sake, will…'. The English-speaker pitfall is the ending: learners write 응원할께요 (wrong spelling — standard is 할게요) or use plain future 응원할 거예요 ('I will cheer', a flat prediction) instead of the promissory 할게요 that conveys personal commitment to the listener. To a senior or in formal settings, raise it to 응원하겠습니다. Register: 응원할게 (banmal) ↔ 응원할게요 (polite) ↔ 응원하겠습니다 (formal).

From 應援: 응원 'support/cheering' + -ㄹ게요 'I will (for you)'.

mistakes: Spelling it 응원할께요 — the standard promissory ending is -ㄹ게요: 응원할게요 (pronounced with a tense 께 sound but written 게).
Using 응원할 거예요 instead — that is a flat prediction 'I will cheer'; the warm promise to the listener is 응원할게요.
Treating it as identical to 화이팅 — 화이팅 is an in-the-moment shout, while 응원할게요 pledges ongoing, personal support.

english: It suits you / It looks good on you.
usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger
examples: A: (새 안경 쓰고) 어때요? / B: 와, 진짜 잘 어울려요!
A: (in new glasses) How is it? / B: Wow, it really suits you!
the go-to reaction to a new look, item, or haircut
원피스 입은 친구한테 "그 옷 너랑 진짜 잘 어울려" 했어요.
To my friend in a dress I said, 'That outfit really suits you.'
everyday: name the item + 너랑 잘 어울려, the natural compliment on clothes
머리 자른 부장님께 "머리 스타일 잘 어울리세요" 했어요.
To the manager's new haircut I said, 'That hairstyle suits you, sir.'
real situation: honorific 잘 어울리세요 toward a senior's look
nuance: 잘 어울려요 (잘 'well' + 어울리다 'to match/go together') is the everyday 'it suits you / it looks good on you' for clothes, glasses, a haircut, makeup, or a color — and the single most natural thing to say when someone shows off a new look. The dividing line from 예뻐요/멋있어요 is key: 예뻐요 judges the THING itself as pretty, while 잘 어울려요 says it MATCHES the person well — so it flatters the wearer, not just the item, which is why Koreans reach for it constantly. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: the particle is 와/과 or colloquial 랑/하고 for 'goes WITH' (그 색이 너랑 잘 어울려, not 너를), and 어울리다 is intransitive, so you never say 어울려요 + object; second, learners drop 잘 and say bare 어울려요, but the warm compliment almost always keeps 잘 ('suits you WELL') — bare 어울리다 alone sounds like a neutral 'matches'. For two people who look good together you can also say 두 사람 잘 어울려요 ('you two make a good couple'). Register: 잘 어울려 (banmal) ↔ 잘 어울려요 (polite) ↔ 잘 어울리세요 (honorific).

mistakes: Using an object particle (그 옷을 잘 어울려요) — 어울리다 is intransitive; the thing 'goes with' you: 그 옷이 너랑/너한테 잘 어울려요.
Dropping 잘 and saying bare 어울려요 — the compliment keeps 잘 ('suits you well'); without it, it sounds like a flat 'it matches'.
Saying 예뻐요 when you mean it flatters the person — 예뻐요 praises the item itself, while 잘 어울려요 says it suits the wearer.
Using bare 잘 어울려 to an elder — raise it to the honorific 잘 어울리세요 when complimenting a senior's outfit or hair.
